title: Joseph: Dreams and Betrayal
rules: Existing native Story wheel, sizing, rewards and three contextual hints (free / 15 / 25 Insight Tokens). Native full reveal costs 25 Points. Development entry only; unlock after Episode 13. No unrelated modes or public loader changes.
completionMessage: Jacob is grieving for a son who's still alive. Joseph has been taken into Egypt and sold to Potiphar, Pharaoh's chief of the guard (Genesis 37:36). His dreams haven't been fulfilled, and his story isn't over. For now, you've reached the end of this episode.

discoveries.title: A Gift That Sets Joseph Apart
discoveries.narration: Joseph is 17 and tends his father's flocks. He's brought a bad report about some of his brothers, and there's already trouble in the family. Jacob loves Joseph especially and has a distinctive garment made for him. His brothers can see the favor, and they can't speak peaceably to him.

interaction.prompt: What special garment made Jacob's favor toward Joseph visible to his brothers?

progressiveHints.text: Think of something Joseph wore, not a piece of shepherding equipment.
Jacob had this item made especially for him.
The NWT also describes it as a beautiful long garment. Build the word for this outer clothing.

discoveries.explanation: Jacob had a special robe made for Joseph because he loved him especially as a son of his old age. Genesis doesn't describe it as a coat of many colors. The brothers' hatred had grown so deep that they couldn't speak peaceably to Joseph. A gift had become part of a painful family division.

discoveries.title: Telling the First Dream
discoveries.narration: Now Joseph tells his brothers about an unusual dream. They're out in a field, gathering cut grain into bundles. His bundle stands upright, while theirs gather around and bow down. Can you see why his brothers connect this picture with someone ruling over them?

interaction.prompt: What are the tied bundles of harvested grain in Joseph's first dream called?

progressiveHints.text: These are gathered stalks from a harvest, not living trees.
The word names bundles of cut grain tied together.
Use the plural: one bundle stands upright while the others bow around it.

discoveries.explanation: Sheaves are bundles of harvested grain. In Joseph's dream, his brothers' sheaves bowed to his, and they understood the picture as him ruling over them. They weren't watching this happen in a real field—it was a dream Joseph related to them. Their response was still more hatred.

discoveries.title: A Second Picture in the Sky
discoveries.narration: The next dream takes us from a field to the sky: the sun, the moon, and 11 smaller lights bow down to Joseph. Jacob rebukes him when he hears it. Yet there's another detail worth noticing—his father keeps the saying in mind.

interaction.prompt: Which heavenly objects numbered 11 in Joseph's second dream?

progressiveHints.text: Leave out the two larger lights; the question asks about the group of 11.
These lights often appear together in the night sky.
The dream names the sun, the moon, and 11 of these.

discoveries.explanation: There were 11 stars, along with the sun and moon. Jacob connected the dream with members of the family bowing to Joseph. He rebuked Joseph but also kept the saying in mind. Notice the difference: the brothers grew jealous, while Jacob didn't simply dismiss what he'd heard.

discoveries.title: Finding His Brothers
discoveries.narration: Jacob sends Joseph from the valley of Hebron to check on his brothers and the flock near Shechem. But they aren't there. A man finds Joseph looking for them in a field and tells him where they've gone. Joseph follows that lead instead of turning for home.

interaction.prompt: Where did Joseph finally find his brothers after looking near Shechem?

progressiveHints.text: This is the second place in his search, not where his father first sent him.
A man in a field had heard the brothers name this destination.
Joseph went after them there; it wasn't Hebron, where his journey began.

discoveries.explanation: Joseph found them at Dothan. He'd first gone toward Shechem, then continued after a man told him where they'd moved. Jacob's request was to learn whether his sons and the flock were well. Joseph followed through on that errand even when the first stop didn't bring him to them.

discoveries.title: Before Joseph Arrives
discoveries.narration: Joseph is still some distance away when his brothers spot him. Before he even reaches them, they begin planning to kill him and make it look as though a wild animal attacked him. This isn't a sudden quarrel after he arrives. They're preparing to harm their own brother.

interaction.prompt: What word means the secret, harmful plan the brothers made before Joseph reached them?

progressiveHints.text: Think of a plan made against someone, rather than an argument that happens by surprise.
They planned both the harm and a false explanation for their father.
Use the noun for a dishonest plan or plot. Here, the brothers intend to hide what they've done.

discoveries.explanation: A scheme is a dishonest or harmful plan. The brothers plotted against Joseph before he reached them, even planning to blame a wild animal. Their hostility had moved beyond words into preparations to take his life. The Bible tells us what they planned; it doesn't approve of it.

discoveries.title: A Plan to Bring Him Home
discoveries.narration: Before Joseph reaches them, his brothers are already plotting to kill him. One brother speaks against taking his life. He suggests putting Joseph into a waterpit without harming him. Genesis lets us know what he's really trying to do: get Joseph safely back to their father.

interaction.prompt: Which brother proposed the waterpit because he intended to rescue Joseph and return him to Jacob?

progressiveHints.text: This brother opposed the plan to take Joseph's life.
His aim was to bring Joseph back to their father, not hand him over to traders.
He proposed using a pit without shedding blood because he intended to rescue Joseph later.

discoveries.explanation: Reuben was trying to rescue Joseph. His suggestion about the pit wasn't the whole plan—Genesis explicitly says he intended to return Joseph to their father. Judah's later proposal was different: sell Joseph. Keeping those two proposals separate helps us follow what each brother actually did.

discoveries.title: An Empty Pit
discoveries.narration: When Joseph arrives, the brothers strip off his special robe and throw him into a pit. There's a small but important detail in the account: it's empty, with no water in it. Joseph is still alive, but his brothers have put him where he can't simply continue his errand.

interaction.prompt: What kind of storage place, empty and dry at the time, did the brothers throw Joseph into?

progressiveHints.text: This was a place meant to hold a liquid, not an animal pen.
It was dug down into the ground, and there was no water inside.
Combine what it normally held with the word for a deep hole. The NWT uses this compound word.

discoveries.explanation: It was a waterpit—a place for holding water—but this one was dry. That detail matters: the brothers had put Joseph into confinement, not into water. They'd also taken his special robe. Reuben's rescue plan hadn't yet succeeded, and Joseph was still in danger.

discoveries.title: Traders on the Road
discoveries.narration: The brothers sit down to eat while Joseph is in the pit. Then they look up and see travelers coming from Gilead, with loaded camels on their way to Egypt. The goods they carry have familiar uses in trade, but their arrival is about to change Joseph's life.

interaction.prompt: What word describes the traveling group of merchants and loaded camels the brothers saw?

progressiveHints.text: Think of people and pack animals making a trading journey together.
This group came from Gilead and was traveling toward Egypt.
It's a traveling company of traders, not the name of a single merchant or his cargo.

discoveries.explanation: A caravan is a group traveling together, often with goods to trade. This one carried labdanum gum, balsam, and resinous bark toward Egypt. The brothers noticed it while they were eating. That trading journey was about to become Joseph's route away from his family.

discoveries.title: Another Brother's Proposal
discoveries.narration: One brother now speaks about the approaching traders. He asks what profit there would be in killing Joseph and hiding what they've done. Instead, he urges them to sell him. He even reminds them that Joseph is their own brother. The others listen to him.

interaction.prompt: Which brother proposed selling Joseph instead of killing him?

progressiveHints.text: This wasn't the brother who intended to rescue Joseph and return him to Jacob.
He asked what profit there would be in killing Joseph and covering over his blood.
He urged them to sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites, reminding them that Joseph was their own flesh.

discoveries.explanation: Judah proposed the sale. He argued against killing Joseph, but selling their brother into slavery was still a terrible wrong. His proposal was different from Reuben's rescue plan: Reuben wanted Joseph home with their father. Judah persuaded the others to hand Joseph over to traders.

discoveries.title: A Brother Sold
discoveries.narration: Joseph is lifted out of the pit, but this isn't the rescue Reuben planned. His brothers sell him for 20 pieces of a precious metal. The traders take Joseph toward Egypt. He's alive, yet the journey ahead is one he hasn't chosen.

interaction.prompt: Which metal was used for the 20 pieces paid when Joseph was sold?

progressiveHints.text: The price wasn't paid in livestock or grain.
It's a precious metal, but the passage doesn't say gold.
The NWT calls the payment 20 pieces of this metal; it doesn't describe minted coins.

discoveries.explanation: Joseph was sold for 20 pieces of silver, and the traders took him toward Egypt. Being brought up out of the pit hadn't meant freedom. His own brothers had sold him into slavery. Genesis calls the payment pieces of silver; it doesn't describe minted coins.

discoveries.title: Too Late to Rescue Him
discoveries.narration: When Reuben returns to the waterpit, Joseph is gone. Reuben tears his garments and goes back to the brothers, distressed about what he'll do now. His plan had been to bring Joseph home. Finding the pit like this tells him that the rescue he intended hasn't happened.

interaction.prompt: What word describes the pit when Reuben returned and found Joseph gone?

progressiveHints.text: The question is about whether Joseph was there, not whether the pit held water.
The traders had already taken Joseph away.
The person he hoped to rescue wasn't there. Use the opposite of occupied.

discoveries.explanation: The pit was empty when Reuben came back. Earlier it had held no water; now Joseph himself was missing. Reuben tore his garments and expressed his distress to the brothers. Genesis doesn't explain where he'd been while Joseph was sold, so we shouldn't invent a reason for his absence.

discoveries.title: A Father's Sorrow
discoveries.narration: The brothers dip Joseph's special robe in a male goat's blood and send it to Jacob to identify. He recognizes it and concludes that a wild animal has killed his son. Jacob mourns for many days. We know Joseph is alive; his father doesn't.

interaction.prompt: What word describes Jacob's deep sorrow as he mourned the son he believed was dead?

progressiveHints.text: This is an emotional response to losing someone, not a name for anger at an enemy.
It explains why words of comfort didn't simply end his mourning.
Think of the deep sorrow people experience when someone they love has died.

discoveries.explanation: Jacob's grief was real, even though Joseph hadn't died. The robe was genuine, but the impression the brothers created was false. Jacob tore his garments, wore sackcloth, and continued weeping despite his family's attempts to comfort him. Their deception had left him mourning a son who was still alive.

The visual is Reuben's intervention (21–22), distinct from Judah's later proposal. His purpose to rescue Joseph and return him to Jacob is explicit. Verses 26–27 support the explanation's comparison with Judah; the rescue had not succeeded.
